nameStory: The Lance Aplexa gets its name from its distinctly elongated, lance-like shell shape that tapers to a sharp point. The genus name 'Sibirenauta' hints at its northern origins, as it was first discovered in Siberian waters before being found in North America.
description: The Lance Aplexa is a small freshwater snail with a distinctive elongated, spiral shell that looks like a tiny twisted spear. This aquatic gastropod belongs to the bladder snail family and is quite rare in New England, with only a handful of confirmed sightings. The shell is typically translucent to pale brown and has a noticeably pointed, lance-like shape that sets it apart from rounder pond snails. These little mollusks are air-breathing snails that live underwater but come to the surface periodically for oxygen.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: The shell is distinctly elongated and lance-like, much more pointed and stretched than typical round pond snails. It feels smooth and delicate when gently handled.

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: Translucent to pale amber-brown coloration that allows you to see through to the snail's body inside. The shell has a glassy, almost crystal-like appearance.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to rest comfortably on your fingernail, typically less than half an inch long. Despite being tiny, the elongated shape makes it appear larger than round snails of similar volume.

idTips.label: Spiral Pattern
idTips.description: The shell spirals are tightly wound and create distinct ridges you can feel with your fingertip. The whorls are more compressed than in typical bladder snails.

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly along surfaces underwater, leaving a barely visible slime trail. Often seen crawling on aquatic plants or the underside of the water surface.

habitat: Lance Aplexa inhabits clean, slow-moving freshwater environments like quiet streams, ponds, and lake edges with abundant aquatic vegetation. Look for them in shallow areas with soft sediments and plenty of submerged plants, particularly in cooler northern waters. They prefer habitats with good water quality and minimal pollution.

seasonality.spring: Active as waters warm, often found crawling on emerging aquatic plants. This is when they're most likely to be spotted near the surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible grazing on algae and plant matter. Look for them on submerged vegetation during warm, calm days.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper waters. May be found on dying aquatic plants before winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, buried in soft sediments or hidden among plant debris at the bottom of water bodies.

funFact: Despite being air-breathing snails that live underwater, Lance Aplexa can create their own diving bell by trapping a bubble of air against their shell, allowing them to stay submerged for extended periods while still accessing oxygen.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small bladder snails, but the Lance Aplexa's distinctly pointed, elongated shell is like comparing a torpedo to a marble. Remember: if it looks like a tiny glass lance, you've found something special.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England with only three confirmed observations, making any sighting scientifically valuable. The rarity means most people will never encounter one, but citizen science reports of unusual elongated freshwater snails are important for tracking this elusive species.
compareHints: Since this is the only Sibirenauta species in the region, compare it to other bladder snails in the Physidae family. Unlike the common bladder snail which has a rounded, bulbous shell, the Lance Aplexa is dramatically more elongated and pointed. Other physid snails in New England have shells that are either more rounded or left-coiling, while the Lance Aplexa maintains its distinctive lance-like profile.
